title: God Has Spoken by His Son
subtitle: Hebrews 1:1–4
description: The sermon opens at the top: God spoke many times and many ways, and in these last days by his Son, heir, maker, radiance, seated.
paragraphs: Every other book in this part of the series opened with a name. Paul signed his letters, Luke explained his method, John began with the Word. This book begins with no greeting, no author, and no address, and its first word is God. It is a sermon that travels as a letter, written to believers who knew the Scriptures of Israel by heart and were in danger of quietly letting go of what they had heard. The series places it in the undated group, because the text gives no date for itself and names no writer, and the telling will not supply what the text withholds. What the text does give, in its very first sentence, is its whole argument in seed form: God has spoken, more than once and in more than one way, and the last and greatest speaking has a name.

The opening sentence sets the old speaking and the new side by side. “On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets.” Many occasions, many ways: dreams and visions, thunder on a mountain, a burning bush, poetry and oracle and story, a long conversation carried on across centuries with a whole people. None of it is dismissed. It was God speaking, and this book will quote those prophets and psalmists on nearly every page as the living voice of God. But it was fragmentary, piece by piece, shadow by shadow, and it was not the end of the sentence. “in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son.” Not by another prophet carrying a message. By a Son, who is himself the message, and the days his coming opens are called, simply, these last days.

Then the sermon stacks the Son's credentials one on another, the way its hearers would stack stones. He is the one “whom He appointed heir of all things, and through whom He made the universe.” Heir of all things: the end of the story belongs to him. Maker of the universe: the beginning of the story ran through him. The writer is not describing a spokesman God sent after the prophets failed. He is describing the one through whom everything exists and to whom everything is going, and saying that when God wanted to speak his final word to the world, he did not send a messenger. He sent him.

And the description climbs higher before it comes down to the cross. “The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of His nature, upholding all things by His powerful word.” Radiance, the shining out of a light, not a reflection borrowed from elsewhere. Exact representation, the stamp that matches the die perfectly, God's nature made visible without loss. And in the present tense, holding the universe up by his word even now. Then, inside the same sentence, the sermon reaches the deed the whole book will circle: “After He had provided purification for sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.” Sat down. Priests in the old order stood, because their work was never finished. This one sat, and the sermon will spend chapters unpacking what that chair means. For now it simply stands in the opening paragraph like a fact the hearers already know and are in danger of forgetting.

The first movement of the argument is announced in one comparative sentence: “He became as far superior to the angels as the name He has inherited is excellent beyond theirs.” Why angels? Because the hearers ranked them high, and rightly: angels had carried God's law and God's appearances all through the old story. The sermon does not lower the angels to raise the Son. It measures the distance. A name inherited, Son, set against names given for service. The next stretch of the sermon will prove the sentence out of the hearers' own Scriptures, psalm by psalm, and everything after that, Moses, Aaron, Melchizedek, covenant, sanctuary, sacrifice, will be measured by the same question this opening asks. How great is the one who has spoken? The first four verses answer with everything the writer has: heir, maker, radiance, exact image, upholder, purifier, seated. The sermon has begun, and it began at the top.

title: Greater Than the Angels
subtitle: Hebrews 1:5–14
description: Psalm by psalm, the sermon proves the Son worshiped and enthroned above the angels, who are ministering spirits sent to serve the heirs.
paragraphs: The opening sentence claimed the Son is as far superior to the angels as his inherited name is beyond theirs, and the sermon now proves the claim the way its hearers would demand: out of their own Scriptures, text by text. No angel is named or blamed. The method is a question no one in the room can answer any way but one. For to which of the angels did God ever say, “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father”? The words are from Psalm 2, spoken to the anointed king, and again from the promise to David about his son: “I will be His Father, and He will be My Son.” Father and Son is a relation God speaks to this one. To no angel, ever, does the record show him saying it.

The proof runs on through the psalms like a chain being pulled link by link. When God brings his firstborn into the world, the command goes out to the other side of the comparison: “Let all God’s angels worship Him.” Angels worship; the Son is worshiped, and the sentence stands in Scripture itself. About the angels God says one thing, and the sermon quotes it fairly: “He makes His angels winds, His servants flames of fire.” Winds and flames, swift, bright, powerful, and made, things God fashions and sends. Then the sermon turns the page to Psalm 45 and sets the contrast down in the open: About the Son he says, “Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever, and justice is the scepter of Your kingdom.” Angels are made winds. The Son is addressed as God, and his throne has no end date written on it.

The chain does not stop at rank; it reaches character and permanence. “You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, Your God, has anointed You above Your companions with the oil of joy.” The anointing above companions is tied to a moral fact, that this king loves what is right and hates what is wicked, and his joy is the overflow of it. Then the sermon reaches Psalm 102, a prayer spoken by an afflicted man to the Lord who made everything, and applies its words to the Son without blinking: “In the beginning, O Lord, You laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands.” The one who laid the foundations stands on the far side of his own creation's decay: “They will perish, but You remain; they will all wear out like a garment.” And the psalm's last word on him: “but You remain the same, and Your years will never end.” Garments get rolled up and changed. He does not change.

The final question returns to the form of the first and closes the case. Yet to which of the angels did God ever say, “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet”? The words are Psalm 110, the most quoted psalm in this whole book, and they match the seated Christ of the sermon's opening paragraph, the one who provided purification and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. No angel was ever offered that seat. And so the sermon can afford to end the movement generously, with the angels restored to their real dignity rather than diminished: “Are not the angels ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation?” Sent to serve the heirs. That is the settled order the first chapter leaves standing: angels are glorious servants on assignment to the people who will inherit salvation, and the Son is the heir himself, worshiped by the servants, seated beside the Majesty, the same yesterday and forever before forever was a word his hearers used. The comparison is closed. What remains is the danger, and the sermon turns to it next without pausing for applause.

title: Pay Attention, Do Not Drift
subtitle: Hebrews 2:1–9
description: The first warning, against drifting, and Psalm 8's promise held against the unsubjected present: yet at present we do not see, but we see Jesus.
paragraphs: The sermon interrupts its own argument, and the interruption is the point. Between the proof that the Son is greater than the angels and everything still to come, the preacher steps out from behind the texts and speaks to the room in the first person plural: “We must pay closer attention, therefore, to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away.” Drift is the danger this whole book is written against. Not rebellion announced out loud, not a door slammed. A slow slide, the way a boat slips its mooring in a current nobody feels. The remedy named is not fear but attention, closer attention, paid on purpose to what they have already heard.

The warning that follows is built as an argument from the lesser to the greater, the sermon's own logic turned on its hearers. “For if the message spoken by angels was binding, and every transgression and disobedience received its just punishment, how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?” The old message, the law carried by angels in the telling Israel knew, held, and its penalties were real. This greater salvation cannot be treated more lightly than the lesser word was. And its credentials are laid out in a chain of custody: “This salvation was first announced by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard Him,” and God himself added his witness, “through signs, wonders, various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to His will.” Announced by the Lord, confirmed by eyewitnesses, affirmed by God. Neglect, not defiance, is the sin named. The word is escape, and the question has no answer supplied, because there is none the sermon will offer.

Then the argument resumes, and it turns a corner a reader might not expect. “For it is not to angels that He has subjected the world to come, about which we are speaking.” The world to come belongs not to angels but to man, and the sermon proves it with a psalm it introduces with a preacher's shrug about its address: Somewhere it is testified, “What is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him?” Psalm 8, the night sky psalm, wonder that the maker of the moon and stars notices human beings at all. “You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor and placed everything under his feet.” Everything means everything: “He left nothing outside of his control.”

And then the sermon does the most honest thing in the chapter. It looks at the world as it stands and refuses to pretend. “Yet at present we do not see everything subject to him.” The psalm says everything is under man's feet; the world outside the window says otherwise, and the preacher says so first, before any hearer can object. The promise and the present do not match, and the sermon holds both in one sentence without flinching from either. That tension is where the hearers live. It is where the drifting starts: the long gap between what God has said about the world to come and what the world at present looks like.

Into that gap the sermon sets one sight it can verify. “But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death, so that by the grace of God He might taste death for everyone.” We do not see everything subjected. But we see Jesus. The psalm's words fit him in the order the psalm gives them: made a little lower than the angels, that is the incarnation and the suffering, then crowned with glory and honor, and the crown came by way of the death. He tasted death, the sermon says, not as a sip but in full, for everyone, by the grace of God. The world to come is not yet visible under man's feet. It is already visible on one man's head, and he wears a crown where the psalm promised one. The sermon's hearers are being taught where to look while they wait: not at the unsubjected world, but at the crowned pioneer standing ahead of them in it.

title: The Pioneer Who Suffered
subtitle: Hebrews 2:10–18
description: Made perfect through suffering, unashamed to call them brothers, destroyer of death's power, a merciful and faithful high priest.
paragraphs: The sermon's next sentence is one of the strangest in the book, and it does not soften it. “In bringing many sons to glory, it was fitting for God, for whom and through whom all things exist, to make the author of their salvation perfect through suffering.” Fitting. The author of salvation, the pioneer who cuts the path the sons will follow, was made perfect through suffering, and God considered that right, the way things should be. The word perfect here does not mean improved from a flaw. It means completed, fitted for the work, a captain made fully ready by going through the whole road himself. The sons are being brought to glory along a path, and the one at the front has walked every step of it in pain.

Because of that shared road, the sermon says something almost startling about how Jesus speaks of the people he saves. “For both the One who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are of the same family. So Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers.” Of one family, the sanctifier and the sanctified, and no shame in the family name. The sermon proves the brotherhood out of the Scriptures again, putting the psalms and Isaiah into the mouth of the Son: “I will proclaim Your name to My brothers; I will sing Your praises in the assembly.” And again, “I will put My trust in Him.” And once again, “Here am I, and the children God has given Me.” Jesus stands in the middle of the congregation singing, one of the family, trusting the Father alongside his brothers, presenting the children as God's gift to him. The distance the first chapter measured between the Son and the angels is real. This chapter measures the closeness he chose between the Son and his people.

The closeness had a cost and a purpose, and both are named. “Now since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death.” Flesh and blood were not a costume. He shared in their humanity, truly one of them, so that his death could strike the one who holds death's power and break the oldest slavery named in the book, the fear of death that runs underneath a whole human life. The deliverance is aimed at people who were not chained by an army but by a fear, and it is won not by avoiding death but by dying. And the sermon is precise about who this help is for: “For surely it is not the angels He helps, but the descendants of Abraham.” The glorious servants of the first chapter get no rescue. The family of Abraham does.

Out of the shared humanity the sermon draws the office the rest of the book will be about. “For this reason He had to be made like His brothers in every way, so that He might become a merciful and faithful high priest in service to God, in order to make atonement for the sins of the people.” Made like his brothers in every way was not a courtesy; it was a requirement, had to be, because the priesthood he was entering runs on resemblance. A priest stands between God and people who are like him, and mercy is his working quality precisely because he knows the country from inside. The words high priest appear here for the first time in the sermon, and they arrive carrying mercy and faithfulness as the job description.

The chapter closes with the pastoral fruit of the whole argument, one sentence long. “Because He Himself suffered when He was tempted, He is able to help those who are being tempted.” Not able to sympathize from a safe distance. Able to help, in the present tense, while the temptation is happening, because his own suffering under temptation is the qualification. The sermon's hearers were tempted to drift, to let go, to turn back toward a safer and smaller faith, and the preacher's answer is not first a threat but a person: a brother who has been where they are, a pioneer who finished the road, a priest who can be approached because he has suffered the same pressure. The warnings in this book are severe, and they are coming. But they are severe words spoken about a Christ who is first introduced as unashamed of his brothers.

title: Greater Than Moses
subtitle: Hebrews 3:1–6
description: Moses faithful as a servant in the house, Christ faithful as the Son over it, and the house identified: we are his house, if we hold firmly.
paragraphs: The sermon now turns its comparison on the most honored name in Israel's story. It begins with the hearers themselves, addressed at their highest: “Therefore, holy brothers, who share in the heavenly calling, set your focus on Jesus, the apostle and high priest whom we confess.” Two titles are set on Jesus in one breath. Apostle, the one sent from God to men. High priest, the one who stands before God for men. The sermon has already spent chapters on the second title's roots, and now it fixes the hearers' attention, set your focus, on the man who carries both. Holy brothers, sharing a calling that comes from heaven: that is who they are told they are before they are warned about anything.

Moses is treated with full honor first, because the comparison only means something if Moses is genuinely great. “He was faithful to the One who appointed Him, just as Moses was faithful in all God’s house.” Jesus faithful, Moses faithful, the same commendation Scripture gives the man who led Israel out of Egypt and received the law on the mountain. The sermon's argument is not that Moses failed. It is arithmetic about position: “For Jesus has been counted worthy of greater glory than Moses, just as the builder of a house has greater honor than the house itself.” A house can be beautiful, and the one who designed and built it still outranks it, and behind the figure stands the largest fact of all: “every house is built by someone, but God is the builder of everything.” Jesus is being placed on the builder's side of the line, with God. Moses stands inside the house he served.

The distinction is then stated as plainly as the sermon ever states anything. “Now Moses was faithful as a servant in all God’s house, testifying to what would be spoken later.” A servant in the house, faithful in the house, and his faithfulness had a forward lean to it: his testimony pointed at things that would be spoken later, beyond his own day. “But Christ is faithful as the Son over God’s house.” Servant in, Son over. The whole difference between the old order and the new sits in those two prepositions. Moses served a house he did not own and testified to a word he did not finish. The Son presides over his own Father's house, and the word Moses testified toward is the word this sermon is preaching.

Then the house itself is identified, and the sentence turns gently and dangerously toward the hearers. “And we are His house, if we hold firmly to our confidence and the hope of which we boast.” We are his house. The building God is raising is not stone; it is these believing people, and the condition is left hanging in the sentence in plain sight: if we hold firmly. The confidence and the boasted hope are not decorations on the house; holding them is what the house's standing consists of. The sermon does not yet call this a threat. It states it as the simple architecture of the thing, the way a builder might state that a wall stands if its footing holds.

That conditional if is the hinge into the sermon's longest warning, and it is worth seeing what the preacher has done before he turns it. In five verses he has honored Moses completely, outranked him completely, and relocated the hearers inside the very house Moses served. Their identity is grander than they may feel: holy brothers, sharers in a heavenly calling, God's house under his Son. The warning that follows will be built out of the wilderness generation, the people who left Egypt under Moses and never entered the rest. The sermon's hearers are being told, before they hear a word of it, whose house they now stand in, and what it would mean to walk out of it the way that generation walked away. The next text is a psalm about a single day, and the day is called today.

title: Today, If You Hear His Voice
subtitle: Hebrews 3:7–19
description: Psalm 95 lands on the present congregation, the wilderness generation held up as a mirror under one word of time: today.
paragraphs: The sermon now quotes a psalm and treats the quotation as a live voice in the room. Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts, as you did in the rebellion, in the day of testing in the wilderness.” Psalm 95 was written centuries after the wilderness, and the sermon insists its first word lands on the present congregation anyway: today. Not the day of Moses, and not only the day of the psalmist. Today, as long as the word is being heard. The rebellion the psalm names is the one Israel's own story tells, the generation that came out of Egypt, tested God through forty years of visible provision, “and for forty years saw My works,” and hardened anyway. God's verdict on that generation stands inside the psalm in his own voice: “They shall never enter My rest.” The sermon does not quote the psalm as history. It quotes it as a warning addressed, this morning, to its hearers.

Then the preacher does the arithmetic of the psalm out loud, question by question, so the room cannot miss who the warning is about. “For who were the ones who heard and rebelled? Were they not all those Moses led out of Egypt?” They heard, with their own ears, the promises and the plagues and the sea splitting, and rebelled anyway. “And with whom was God angry for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness?” Angry for forty years, the whole span of the wandering, until the generation that left Egypt lay buried in the desert it had chosen. “And to whom did He swear that they would never enter His rest? Was it not to those who disobeyed?” Heard and rebelled, sinned and fell, disobeyed and shut out. The conclusion is drawn in one flat sentence at the end of the chapter: “So we see that it was because of their unbelief that they were unable to enter.” Not because the promise failed, and not because the road was too hard. Because of unbelief. They were unable to enter, and the inability is traced to a heart condition, not a circumstance.

Between the psalm and the arithmetic, the sermon sets down the pastoral practice the whole book runs on. “See to it, brothers, that none of you has a wicked heart of unbelief that turns away from the living God.” See to it is plural work, a congregation charged with watching one another's hearts, because the danger named is not a sudden apostasy but a heart quietly turning away from the living God while still sitting in the room. And the watch has a daily rhythm and a deadline woven into the same word the psalm opened with: “But exhort one another daily, as long as it is called today, so that none of you may be hardened by sin’s deceitfulness.” Exhort one another daily. Sin deceives, and the deception hardens gradually, and the antidote the sermon prescribes is not solitary effort but a community that speaks to each other every day the day is still called today.

The chapter's other sentence of condition belongs here too: “We have come to share in Christ if we hold firmly to the end the assurance we had at first.” Come to share, a settled sharing already given, and the firm holding to the end is how that sharing shows itself real. The sermon is not teaching its hearers to purchase a place by endurance. It is teaching them to recognize the genuine thing by its perseverance, the way the wilderness generation is recognized in reverse: they started with every advantage, the sea, the manna, the mountain, and their unbelief at the end revealed what their hearts had been doing all along. The psalm's line is repeated once more inside the application, like a refrain the preacher will not let the room forget: “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts, as you did in the rebellion.”

So the third chapter leaves the hearers standing where Israel stood, with better promises and the same choice, and one word of time hanging over the whole congregation. Today is not a date on a calendar in this sermon. It is the name of the season in which God is speaking and a heart can still stay soft. Tomorrow, in the psalm's arithmetic, the wilderness generation also expected to decide, and their todays ran out one funeral at a time until the oath stood: they shall never enter my rest. The sermon will spend its next movement asking what that rest even is, and whether it still stands open. The answer begins with the same word. There remains a rest, and the day to enter it is still called today.

title: The Rest That Remains
subtitle: Hebrews 4:1–13
description: God's rest predates the refusal and survives it: a Sabbath rest remains, entered by believing, examined by a living and active word.
paragraphs: The wilderness generation heard the same opening word the congregation has heard, and the sermon begins this movement by refusing to let the parallel sit quietly. “Therefore, while the promise of entering His rest still stands, let us be careful that none of you be deemed to have fallen short of it.” The promise still stands: that is the sermon's first point, and it is astonishing. The rest God swore that generation would never enter was not withdrawn from the world. It was forfeited by them, and it stands open still, and standing open it carries its own fear, that a person might be deemed to have fallen short of it while it was within reach. The danger is not that the door is closed. The danger is arriving too careless to walk through it.

Why did the first hearers miss it? The sermon answers with a sentence about hearing itself. “For we also received the good news just as they did; but the message they heard was of no value to them, since they did not share the faith of those who comprehended it.” The good news existed in the wilderness, the promise of rest preached to that generation in its own form, and the hearing did them no good because the word landed without faith to mix with it. Hearing is not entering. The sermon keeps pressing this distinction because its hearers are professional hearers, people in the room every week, and the wilderness generation is being held up as the photograph of religious people the word passed through without taking hold. Against them stands the sermon's quiet counter-claim: “Now we who have believed enter that rest.” Believing and entering are the same motion in this book.

Then the preacher does something unexpected: he proves the rest still exists out of Genesis, by setting two ancient sentences side by side. God swore in the psalm, “They shall never enter My rest.” Yet of God's own rest it is written, “And on the seventh day God rested from all His works.” The rest exists; God entered it at creation's end, long before the wilderness generation refused it. A rest that predates the refusal cannot have been cancelled by the refusal. And the psalm's very lateness argues the same: David spoke of entering, centuries after Joshua led Israel into the land, and so, “For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day.” The conquest of Canaan was real, and it was not the rest. Another day was still being announced in David's time, which means it is still being announced in the sermon's time, and the day's name has not changed: today.

The conclusion is one of the book's most quoted sentences, and it is stated as simple arithmetic: “There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God.” Remains. After creation's seventh day, after the wilderness refusal, after Joshua, after David, a Sabbath rest is still on the table for the people of God, “For whoever enters God’s rest also rests from his own work, just as God did from His.” And the response the sermon asks for is a paradox it states without embarrassment: “Let us, therefore, make every effort to enter that rest, so that no one will fall by following the same pattern of disobedience.” Make every effort to enter a rest. Strive, so as not to fall by disobedience, toward the ceasing of your own works. The effort is not earning; it is the refusal to drift, the whole congregation rowing toward the one harbor where rowing ends.

The movement closes with the most famous description of Scripture in the New Testament, set here not as decoration but as the instrument of the whole examination. “For the word of God is living and active. Sharper than any double-edged sword, it pierces even to dividing soul and spirit, joints and marrow. It judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” The word these hearers keep hearing is not inert information they can admire and file. It cuts, to the joints of a person, to the intentions underneath the thoughts, the motives a man hides even from himself. And no one stands outside the examination: “everything is uncovered and exposed before the eyes of Him to whom we must give account.” The sermon has moved from psalm to promise to anatomy in thirteen verses, and its hearers are left with a rest still standing open, a word still cutting, and a God before whom nothing is covered. The next sentence will not leave them exposed and comfortless. It begins, therefore, since we have a great high priest.

title: A Great High Priest
subtitle: Hebrews 4:14–5:10
description: A great high priest passed through the heavens, able to sympathize, called by God like Aaron, who learned obedience through loud cries and tears.
paragraphs: After the exposed heart of the last movement, the sermon sets down the sentence its hearers most need, and it is the hinge the whole book swings on. “Therefore, since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold firmly to what we profess.” Passed through the heavens: the picture is of the old high priest passing through the curtain into the Holy of Holies once a year, lifted now to its true scale, God's own Son gone through the heavens themselves into the real presence. And the response asked is the book's recurring one, grip: hold firmly to the confession. The exposure of the last chapter is not the last word. Between the hearers and the God before whom all is uncovered stands a priest, and he is theirs.

His qualification for their case is stated in the negative first, and it is one of the most tender sentences in the book. “For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin.” Sympathize is not too strong a word for the text; it is the text's own claim. The priest knows weakness from inside, temptation in every way, the full range of it, and the one difference is marked without explanation, yet was without sin. Because of that sympathy, the sermon issues the boldest invitation in the book: “Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need.” A throne, and its name is grace. Mercy for what is past, grace for the present need, and confidence as the manner of approaching. This book contains warnings that can make a reader tremble, and it also contains this door, held open by the preacher on purpose, right after the warnings.

Then the sermon explains what a high priest is, from the old order upward, so the hearers can feel the weight of the title it has given Jesus. “Every high priest is appointed from among men to represent them in matters relating to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.” From among men: the priest belongs to the people he represents. “He is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and misguided, since he himself is subject to weakness.” Gentleness is built into the office by the priest's own frailty, and the frailty has its cost: he must offer for his own sins as well as the people's. And the office is never seized: “No one takes this honor upon himself; he must be called by God, just as Aaron was.” A priest is appointed, not ambitious. The sermon establishes the job's whole shape before it says another word about Jesus, because the shape is the argument.

Measured against that shape, Christ's priesthood is shown to be of the same kind and a higher order at once. “So also Christ did not take upon Himself the glory of becoming a high priest, but He was called by the One who said to Him: ’You are My Son; today I have become Your Father.’” Called, not self-appointed, and called with two texts: the Son text from Psalm 2, and then the one this book will spend a whole chapter unfolding: “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” Forever, and in an order older than Aaron. And the gentleness qualification, the shared weakness, is found in him in a form the old order never knew: “During the days of Jesus’ earthly life, He offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverence.” Loud cries and tears. The sermon's high priest is not gentle by temperament alone; he has prayed in anguish to the God who could save him from death, and submitted when the answer was the cross.

The paradox is stated in eight words and left standing: “Although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered.” A Son, who had never disobeyed, learned obedience, not as information but as experience, by suffering the full cost of obeying where obedience hurt. “And having been made perfect, He became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey Him,” designated by God a high priest in the order of Melchizedek. The sermon has now assembled its whole subject in one place: a great high priest, sympathetic, called, perfected through suffering, the source of an eternal salvation. The preacher pauses here, and his next words are not about Christ at all. They are about the congregation's ears, and they sting.

title: Milk, Solid Food, and a Warning
subtitle: Hebrews 5:11–6:12
description: Dull of hearing rebuked, the elementary foundation honored and left, the falling-away warning at full strength, and beloved spoken over the same people.
paragraphs: The preacher stops mid-argument and complains about his congregation, and the complaint is the doorway into the book's most severe warning. “We have much to say about this, but it is hard to explain, because you are dull of hearing.” The Melchizedek teaching is deep, and the obstacle is not the subject's difficulty but the hearers' condition: dull of hearing, ears gone sluggish from disuse. The rebuke sharpens into a picture nobody in the room wanted: “Although by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to reteach you the basic principles of God’s word. You need milk, not solid food!” By this time: they have had years, teaching enough to be teachers, and instead they need the alphabet retaught. Milk is not condemned; infants need milk. The scandal is adults still needing it, “still an infant, inexperienced in the message of righteousness,” while the food of the mature sits untouched: “But solid food is for the mature, who by constant use have trained their senses to distinguish good from evil.” Maturity in this sermon is not information hoarded but senses trained by constant use, a moral palate built by practice.

The preacher's answer to the dullness is not despair but a push forward. “Therefore let us leave the elementary teachings about Christ and go on to maturity, not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith in God.” The foundation is listed with care, repentance, faith, instruction about baptisms, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment, every item precious and every item a beginning. Foundations are for building on, not for relaying forever, and the sermon announces its intention plainly: “And this we will do, if God permits.” Then, without transition music, it walks straight into the hardest sentences in the book, and they must be carried at the strength the text gives them. “It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have shared in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the coming age,” and then have fallen away, “to be restored to repentance, because they themselves are crucifying the Son of God all over again and subjecting Him to open shame.”

The description of those who fall is deliberately maximal. Enlightened, tasters of the heavenly gift, sharers in the Holy Spirit, tasters of the word's goodness and the coming age's powers: the sermon piles up the fullest possible experience of the faith before it names the fall, so no hearer can comfort himself that the warning concerns people with a thinner religion than his. And the reason given for the impossibility is not a rule about God's willingness but an act the fallen are performing in the present tense: crucifying the Son of God all over again, on their own account, and holding him up to public shame, siding openly with the verdict that crucified him the first time. The text does not soften this, and neither does this telling: the sermon treats a settled, knowing repudiation of Christ by those who have known the full taste of him as a state from which repentance does not come, because repentance is the very thing being repudiated. Land is then made to preach the same sermon in a picture. Rain falls on both fields alike: “land that drinks in the rain often falling on it and that produces a crop useful to those for whom it is tended receives the blessing of God.” But land that produces thorns and thistles is worthless, and its curse is imminent. In the end it will be burned.” Same rain, two harvests, and the difference lies in what the ground does with what it is given.

And then, astonishingly, the preacher's tone turns on a single word: beloved. “Even though we speak like this, beloved, we are convinced of better things in your case,” and he names what he means, “things that accompany salvation.” The warning was meant in earnest, and so is the confidence. This is the only place in the book the hearers are called beloved, and it lands immediately after the fire. The ground of the confidence is not their feelings but their record: “For God is not unjust. He will not forget your work and the love you have shown for His name as you have ministered to the saints and continue to do so.” God is not unjust; their love shown to his people is on his books and will not be forgotten by him. What the preacher asks in return is endurance of the same quality: “We want each of you to show this same diligence to the very end, in order to make your hope sure,” not sluggish, the very word used of their hearing, “but will imitate those who through faith and patience inherit what has been promised.” The warning and the embrace are one pastoral act. The sermon intends its people frightened out of drifting and comforted out of despair in the same ten minutes, and it trusts them to hold both.

title: An Anchor for the Soul
subtitle: Hebrews 6:13–20
description: Promise and oath, two unchangeable things from the God who cannot lie, and hope as an anchor fixed behind the curtain where the forerunner entered.
paragraphs: The sermon now proves that hoping to the end is a reasonable thing to do, and it proves it from the story of Abraham and the character of God. “When God made His promise to Abraham, since He had no one greater to swear by, He swore by Himself, saying, ’I will surely bless you and multiply your descendants.’” An oath needs a greater party to swear by, and there is no one greater than God, so God put himself under his own word, swearing by his own name. The promise to Abraham already carried God's word; the oath was added on top, pure surplus, given for the hearer's sake and not because the word was weak. “And so Abraham, after waiting patiently, obtained the promise.” Waiting patiently is named as the road the promise traveled: years of it, a dead body and a barren womb in the middle of it, and at the far end, the son. The preacher's hearers, urged in the last movement to imitate those who through faith and patience inherit the promises, are being shown the first of those imitators, and his story is told in one verse so they cannot miss the pattern.

Then the sermon explains the oath's purpose with a lawyer's care. Among men, “their oath serves as a confirmation to end all argument,” a sworn word that closes dispute. God's oath works the same way, at his own initiative: “So when God wanted to make the unchanging nature of His purpose very clear to the heirs of the promise, He guaranteed it with an oath.” Wanted to make very clear. The clarity was God's desire, aimed at the heirs, people who did not yet hold the thing promised and needed grounds to keep holding on. What they got was redundancy of the strongest kind: “Thus by two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us may be strongly encouraged.” Two unchangeable things, the promise and the oath, and underneath both, a flat statement about God's nature: it is impossible for God to lie. Strong encouragement is the designed outcome. The sermon that contains the book's sternest warning also contains this engineering of assurance, and both are aimed at the same people.

Out of that assurance comes the picture every sailor in the ancient world would feel in his hands. “We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain.” An anchor does not hold a ship by being seen; often it is out of sight entirely, down in the deep or fixed in the rock, and the ship above the waves is held by something it cannot watch. This anchor is stranger still: it does not go down, it goes in and up, into the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, the Holy of Holies, the one room in the old order where only the high priest went, once a year, alone. The hope of these believers is not anchored to their feelings, their record, or their grip. It is anchored inside the most holy place in existence, fixed where it cannot drag. And the reason it holds there is a person who has already gone in: “where Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf. He has become a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.”

Forerunner is a scout's word, one who goes ahead of the company into a place the company will follow. Jesus has entered the sanctuary not as a solitary exception but on our behalf, the first of a company, and the anchor chain runs from the hearers' souls to the spot where he stands. The chapter ends where the fifth chapter paused, with the name and the order that the dull of hearing were not ready for: a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek. The sermon has spent a full movement anchoring its people, promise, oath, patience, hope, forerunner, so that they can bear the weight of the deep teaching now to come. The anchor is set. The preacher takes a breath and goes back to Genesis, to a king with no genealogy who blessed Abraham in a valley, and the deepest water in the book.

title: A Priest Forever like Melchizedek
subtitle: Hebrews 7
description: Melchizedek argues a priesthood older than Levi's: no genealogy, an indestructible life, God's own oath, and a priest who always lives to intercede.
paragraphs: The sermon now takes up the name it has twice dangled before its hearers, and it begins by simply retelling what Genesis records, nothing more. “This Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of God Most High. He met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him,” and Abraham gave him a tenth of everything. A king and a priest in one person, in Jerusalem's early days under its old name, before Levi was born, before Aaron, before the law. Then the sermon reads the man's name and city the way its hearers were trained to read: “First, his name means ’king of righteousness.’ Then also, ’king of Salem’ means ’king of peace.’” Righteousness first, then peace, the order noted and kept. And then comes the observation the whole chapter is built on, an argument from what the Scripture does not say: “Without father or mother or genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life, like the Son of God, he remains a priest for all time.” Genesis introduces every other figure with a lineage and dismisses them with a death. For Melchizedek it records neither a birth nor a burial, no father, no mother, no first day and no last, and the sermon reads that silence as a portrait: in the text as it stands, he simply remains, a priest without a term, resembling the Son of God in the page's own shape. The telling adds nothing to him, because the argument depends on adding nothing.

From the portrait the sermon argues rank, and the evidence is Abraham himself. “Consider how great Melchizedek was: Even the patriarch Abraham gave him a tenth of the plunder.” The patriarch, the father of the nation, the holder of the promises, paid the tithe, and Melchizedek blessed him, and the sermon's rule is stated as beyond dispute: “indisputably, the lesser is blessed by the greater.” Run that forward through the generations and the consequence is startling: Levi, the tribe that would one day collect tithes from Israel, was still unborn, still in the loins of his ancestor, when Abraham paid. In Abraham, Levi himself paid the tenth to this priest who is not of Levi's line at all. The sermon is not diminishing Levi; it is placing him, precisely, under a priesthood older and greater than his own, with Abraham as the witness who cannot be argued with.

Then the question the whole book turns on is asked in the open. “Now if perfection could have been attained through the Levitical priesthood,” why did Psalm 110, written long after the law, promise another priest in Melchizedek's order and not Aaron's? The very existence of the promise is the verdict: the old priesthood could not finish the job. And a change of priesthood is no small repair, because priesthood and law stand or fall together: “For when the priesthood is changed, the law must be changed as well.” The new priest's credentials break every rule of the old succession on purpose. He belongs to Judah, “a tribe as to which Moses said nothing about priests,” a tribe that never served at the altar. He holds office “not by a law of succession, but by the power of an indestructible life,” and over him stands the testimony the sermon has quoted twice already: “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” The former commandment is therefore set aside, and the sermon gives its reason without flinching: it “was weak and useless (for the law made nothing perfect), and a better hope is introduced, by which we draw near to God.” Made nothing perfect. By which we draw near. The law's failure and the hope's nearness are stated in one breath, because the second is the answer to the first.

Last, the sermon sets the old priesthood and the new side by side in their endings. The Levitical priests became priests without an oath, and there were many of them, “since death prevented them from continuing in office,” a relay race of mortal men handing the office from coffin to coffin. This priest was installed by God's own oath: “The Lord has sworn and will not change His mind: ’You are a priest forever.’” One priest, forever, by oath, and so: “Because of this oath, Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant.” And his permanence is aimed at the present need of wavering people: “But because Jesus lives forever, He has a permanent priesthood. Therefore He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them.” Save completely, and always lives to intercede, always in the present tense. He needs no daily sacrifices, first for his own sins, because he has none: “He sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered up Himself.” The law appoints weak men; “the oath, which came after the law, appointed the Son, who has been made perfect forever.” The deepest water in the book turns out to be an assurance: on the far side of it stands a priest who cannot die out of office, praying for his people at this moment, and a covenant whose guarantee is God sworn.

title: A Better Covenant
subtitle: Hebrews 8
description: Jeremiah's new covenant quoted whole: laws inscribed on hearts, all knowing him from least to greatest, sins remembered no more, the first obsolete.
paragraphs: The sermon stops to underline its own main point, in case the Melchizedek depths have fogged it. “The point of what we are saying is this: We do have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, and who ministers in the sanctuary and true tabernacle set up by the Lord, not by man.” We do have such a high priest. Present possession, not future hope. And where he ministers matters as much as who he is: the true tabernacle, pitched by the Lord and not by man, the original of which the earthly sanctuary was only the working model. Every high priest must have something to offer, the sermon notes, and if Jesus were on earth he would not be a priest at all, since the law's priests already fill that roster. His service is in the real place, and the earthly priests, for all their God-given dignity, serve in what the sermon calls “a copy and shadow of what is in heaven.”

The copy was never a fraud; it was a pattern, and the sermon proves that from the instructions given to Moses himself on the mountain: “See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.” God showed Moses a pattern and required the copy to match it, which means the heaven-side reality existed first and the tabernacle was built downstream of it. A shadow is cast by something solid, and a copy testifies to an original. The old order's glory was always borrowed glory, and it knew it. Now the sermon's comparison completes itself: “Jesus has received a much more excellent ministry, just as the covenant He mediates is better and is founded on better promises.” More excellent ministry, better covenant, better promises, and a mediator standing between God and the people with both parties' interests in his hands. Everything in this book is measured along this one axis: not old against new as enemies, but shadow against substance, promise against the thing promised.

Why a second covenant at all? The sermon asks the question a loyal hearer would ask and answers it with a concession that cuts: “For if that first covenant had been without fault, no place would have been sought for a second.” And then it locates the fault exactly, and not where a careless reader might put it: “But God found fault with the people and said.” The covenant's weakness was the people who kept breaking it. What follows is the longest single quotation in the book, Jeremiah 31, God's own announcement of the covenant that would replace the broken one: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah.” A new covenant, made with the same houses, Israel and Judah, not with strangers. The new is not God's change of people. It is his change of method with the same people.

The difference is stated from inside the old covenant's own story. “It will not be like the covenant I made with their fathers when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, because they did not abide by My covenant.” The Exodus covenant was carried from outside: law on stone, held by a people whose hearts kept wandering off. The new one runs the other direction: “For this is the covenant I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord. I will put My laws in their minds and inscribe them on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people.” Laws in minds, inscribed on hearts, God's own handwriting moving from tablets to the inside of the person. And knowledge of God stops being a taught specialty: “No longer will each one teach his neighbor or his brother,” saying know the Lord, “because they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest.” Least to greatest, the whole range of the people knowing him directly. And beneath it all, the foundation promise the entire book has been approaching: “For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more.” Forgiveness first, memory of sins ended by God's own decision, and hearts re-inscribed as the fruit of it rather than its price.

The chapter closes with the sermon's verdict on the first covenant, delivered in one level sentence that its hearers must have felt in their stomachs. “By speaking of a new covenant, He has made the first one obsolete; and what is obsolete and aging will soon disappear.” Made obsolete by a word: the moment God said new, the first was dated, and what is obsolete and aging will soon disappear. The telling leaves the sentence where the sermon leaves it, as a statement about covenants and not a verdict on a people: the God who made the first covenant is the God who announced the second, to the same houses, from inside the same Scriptures, and the new covenant's entire content is his mercy moving inward. The sermon now turns from the covenant to its machinery, the sanctuary where the old one was served and the single offering by which the new one was sealed, and the next movement opens the tabernacle door and walks inside.

title: Shadows of the Sanctuary
subtitle: Hebrews 9:1–14
description: The tabernacle's rooms, rationed access, and conscience-blind sacrifices preach not yet, until Christ enters the greater tabernacle once for all by his own blood.
paragraphs: The sermon now walks its hearers through the old sanctuary itself, room by room, the way you would walk visitors through a house you grew up in. “Now the first covenant had regulations for worship and also an earthly sanctuary.” A tabernacle was prepared, and the description is unhurried and exact. “In its first room were the lampstand, the table, and the consecrated bread. This was called the Holy Place.” Behind the second curtain stood the Most Holy Place, holding the golden altar of incense and the gold-covered ark of the covenant, and inside the ark three memorials: the gold jar of manna, Aaron's staff that had budded, and the stone tablets of the covenant. Above the ark, the cherubim of glory overshadowed the mercy seat. The preacher knows every object and what it means, and waves off the full tour with a preacher's aside: “But we cannot discuss these things in detail now.” The furniture is not the sermon. The traffic pattern is.

Who could go where, and how often, is the argument. “When everything had been prepared in this way, the priests entered regularly into the first room to perform their sacred duties. But only the high priest entered the second room, and then only once a year, and never without blood, which he offered for himself and for the sins the people had committed in ignorance.” Many priests, the outer room, every day. One priest, the inner room, one day a year, carrying blood, and even he had to offer for his own sins first. Access to God in the old order was real, and it was rationed down to a single man on a single morning, behind a curtain no one else ever passed. The sermon draws the conclusion the architecture itself was preaching: “By this arrangement the Holy Spirit was showing that the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been disclosed as long as the first tabernacle was still standing.” The building was a sermon in cloth and gold, and its text was: not yet, not this way, not for everyone.

And the sacrifices offered inside that arrangement carried a limit the sermon states flatly. The whole setup “is an illustration for the present time, because the gifts and sacrifices being offered were unable to cleanse the conscience of the worshiper.” Unable to cleanse the conscience. They dealt with food and drink and washings, external regulations for the body's cleanness, imposed “until the time of reform,” and a man could leave the tabernacle ceremonially clean and go home with his conscience exactly as burdened as he came. The old order's ceiling was not hypocrisy; it was design. It could manage the outside of a worshiper and testify, by its own arrangement, that the inside still waited for something it could not supply.

Then the sermon sets Christ inside the same floor plan, enlarged to its true scale. “But when Christ came as high priest of the good things that have come, He went through the greater and more perfect tabernacle that is not made by hands and is not a part of this creation.” Not made by hands, not part of this creation: the real sanctuary the copies copied. And his entry was made once, with a better blood than the old room ever saw: “He did not enter by the blood of goats and calves, but He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption.” Once for all, the sermon's hammer phrase, against once a year. His own blood, against blood that was not the priest's own. Eternal redemption, secured, a finished acquisition and not an annual renewal.

The closing comparison argues from the lesser upward one final time. If the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer could sanctify the ceremonially unclean so their bodies were clean, “how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God, purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God!” The very thing the old sacrifices could not reach, the conscience, is the thing this offering reaches. And the goal is not merely a quiet conscience but a freed one: purified from works of death so that we may serve the living God. The shadow sanctuary with its rationed access and its unconsoling sacrifices has done its work. It taught Israel what access costs, what it cannot do, and what to watch for. Now the substance has walked through the greater tabernacle, and the sermon will spend its next movement on the legal heart of the matter: a covenant, like a will, takes effect through death, and the death has happened.

title: Appointed to Die Once
subtitle: Hebrews 9:15–28
description: A will takes effect through death: the covenant ratified in blood, heaven itself entered, man appointed to die once, and a second appearing eagerly awaited.
paragraphs: The sermon now names what the sanctuary tour was approaching: “Therefore Christ is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, now that He has died to redeem them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.” Mediator, inheritance, redemption, and one death reaching backward as well as forward: the transgressions committed under the first covenant, centuries of them, are among the things his death redeems. Then the preacher pauses to explain a word, because the word for covenant is also the word for a will, and the double meaning does legal work. “In the case of a will, it is necessary to establish the death of the one who made it, because a will does not take effect until the one who made it has died; it cannot be executed while he is still alive.” An inheritance passes only through a death. The new covenant's promised eternal inheritance required the death of the one who made it, and Christ's death is therefore not an accident that befell the covenant from outside. It is the covenant's own activating event.

Blood, in fact, runs under both covenants from their first day. “That is why even the first covenant was not put into effect without blood.” The sermon retells the ratification at Sinai: Moses proclaimed every commandment to all the people, took the blood of calves and goats with water, scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled the scroll and all the people, “saying, ’This is the blood of the covenant, which God has commanded you to keep.’” The book, the people, the tabernacle, the vessels, all sprinkled, because the sermon's summary of the law is absolute: “According to the law, in fact, nearly everything must be purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.” Nearly everything, and on the point of forgiveness, no exception at all. The copies of the heavenly things were purified with those sacrifices, “but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these.” The real sanctuary required a real cleansing, and animal blood was never going to be the instrument for heaven itself.

Where Christ entered is then stated against where he did not. “For Christ did not enter a man-made copy of the true sanctuary, but He entered heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God.” Heaven itself, on our behalf, now: the present tense again, a living ministry in the real presence, not a memory of one. And the frequency argument reaches its sharpest form. He did not enter “to offer Himself again and again, as the high priest enters the Most Holy Place every year with blood that is not his own. Otherwise, Christ would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But now He has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself.” Once for all, at the end of the ages: the sermon locates the single offering at history's climax, neither repeatable nor in need of repetition, because the one offering it was himself, and he is not consumed by it.

Then the sermon sets Christ's once inside the pattern of every human life: “Just as man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment, so also Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many; and He will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him.” Die once, then judgment: that is the human appointment, stated without exception. Christ was offered once, fitted into the pattern at its one load-bearing point, bearing the sins of many in his single death. And the pattern's symmetry announces his return: a second appearing, with the errand reversed, not to bear sin, which the first appearing finished, but to bring salvation, completed and final, to those who eagerly await him. The eagerly is doing quiet work. The people this sermon addresses are not dreading the second appearing; the preacher trains them to await it the way heirs await an inheritance that a death has already made legally theirs, because a death has. The chapter that began with a mediator and a will ends with a people looking up, and that posture is exactly what the sermon wants to produce in its wavering hearers: not fear of his coming, but eagerness for it.

title: Once for All
subtitle: Hebrews 10:1–18
description: Standing priests and a seated one: shadows that remind, a body prepared to do God's will, a single offering that made perfect for all time.
paragraphs: The sermon opens its tenth chapter by closing the case on the law's sacrifices, and the verdict is in the first sentence: “For the law is only a shadow of the good things to come, not the realities themselves. It can never, by the same sacrifices offered year after year, make perfect those who draw near to worship.” Never and year after year are the load-bearing words. Repetition is the law's own confession: a sacrifice that must be offered again next year announces, by being offered again, that this year's did not finish the work. The sermon presses the logic to its end. “If it could, would not the offerings have ceased? For the worshipers would have been cleansed once for all, and would no longer have felt the guilt of their sins.” A finished cleansing would end the offerings and clear the conscience in one stroke. Instead, “those sacrifices are an annual reminder of sins, because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.” Annual reminder. The Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the old year, functioned in the end as a yearly appointment with the memory of guilt, because animal blood cannot do what only one offering could.

Into that impossibility the sermon places the voice of Christ himself, arriving in the world and speaking a psalm, Psalm 40, as his own script. “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but a body You prepared for Me. In burnt offerings and sin offerings You took no delight.” The psalmist's words become, in the sermon's reading, the Son's words at his coming: God's desire was never the offerings as such, and the preparation that mattered was a body. Then the purpose of the body is spoken: “Here I am, it is written about Me in the scroll: I have come to do Your will, O God.” The sermon then glosses its own quotation with unusual directness, so no hearer can slide past it: “He takes away the first to establish the second.” The first order of sacrifice is taken away by the second thing, the doing of God's will in a prepared body, and the exchange is not the sermon's invention; it is the psalm's own logic read aloud. The result is stated as an accomplished fact about the hearers themselves: “And by that will, we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.”

The picture that follows is painted in posture. “Day after day every priest stands to minister and to offer again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God.” Stands, day after day, again and again, never: the verbs pile up the old order's endless labor. Sat down: the sermon's opening image returns, finished, one sacrifice for all time, and from the seat he waits, “for His enemies to be made a footstool for His feet.” And the achievement of the single offering is stated with the whole book's tension inside it: “because by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified.” Made perfect, for all time, a completed act. Being sanctified, an ongoing process. The sermon holds both without blinking: the offering's work on their standing is finished forever, and the working of it into their lives continues daily, and neither half cancels the other.

The Holy Spirit is then called as the final witness, and his testimony is the new covenant text from Jeremiah one more time, heard now at the other end of the argument: “This is the covenant I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord. I will put My laws in their hearts and inscribe them on their minds.” And then the clause the whole sanctuary argument was traveling toward: “Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more.” The conclusion lands like a door closing, gently and for good: “And where these have been forgiven, an offering for sin is no longer needed.” No longer needed. Not discouraged, not improved upon, ended, because its purpose stands achieved. The sermon has now said its whole doctrinal word: a better priest, a better covenant, a better sanctuary, a single better sacrifice, and sins remembered no more by the God who swore it. Everything after this point in the book is application, and it begins with the word therefore and an open door.

title: Draw Near, and Do Not Throw Away
subtitle: Hebrews 10:19–39
description: Draw near, hold fast, stir one another up, beside the sternest warning in the book and a congregation reminded of the days it accepted loss with joy.
paragraphs: The doctrine ends and the sermon turns to its people with three commands that structure the Christian life in this book. The ground is stated first: “Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body, and since we have a great priest over the house of God, let us draw near.” Confidence to enter the room only one man a year ever entered, by a way called new and living, opened through the curtain of his body. So the first command is approach: “let us draw near with a sincere heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.” The second is grip: “Let us hold resolutely to the hope we profess, for He who promised is faithful.” And the third is corporate: “And let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds. Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit, but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching.” Draw near, hold fast, stir one another up. Even the attendance warning sits inside the pattern: some had made a habit of staying away, and the sermon treats the habit itself as a spiritual event, because the encouragement that keeps hearts soft happens in the gathering or it does not happen.

Immediately, and in the same breath, stands the book's sternest passage since chapter six, and it is aimed at a precise act. “If we deliberately go on sinning after we have received the knowledge of the truth, no further sacrifice for sins remains, but only a fearful expectation of judgment and of raging fire that will consume all adversaries.” Deliberately go on sinning, after receiving the knowledge of the truth, is not weakness or a fall; it is a settled course chosen with the lights on, and the sermon's logic is bare: if the one sacrifice is spurned, there is no other sacrifice to appeal to, because there is no other. The old comparison follows. Under Moses, a man who rejected the law “died without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” “How much more severely do you think one deserves to be punished who has trampled on the Son of God, profaned the blood of the covenant that sanctified him, and insulted the Spirit of grace?” Trampled, profaned, insulted: the vocabulary is of contempt acted out, a public verdict against the Son and his blood and the Spirit, from a man the blood had sanctified. The sermon knows whose mouth spoke the sanctions: “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,” and again, “The Lord will judge His people.” And the summary line has echoed through centuries of preaching because it earns its dread honestly: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.”

Then the preacher does what a wise pastor does with a frightened and drifting people. He reminds them who they have already been. “Remember the early days that you were in the light. In those days, you endured a great conflict in the face of suffering.” They had stood in public ridicule and persecution, stood beside others being treated so, “sympathized with those in prison and joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property, knowing that you yourselves had a better and permanent possession.” Joyfully accepted the confiscation of their property. This congregation is not being asked to become brave people; they are being reminded that bravery is already in their record, back when the faith was new and cost them goods and standing and they paid with joy because they knew what they owned in heaven. The exhortation is therefore memory before it is effort: “So do not throw away your confidence; it holds a great reward. You need to persevere, so that after you have done the will of God, you will receive what He has promised.”

Over the whole appeal the sermon sets Habakkuk's clock. “In just a little while, He who is coming will come and will not delay. But My righteous one will live by faith; and if he shrinks back, I will take no pleasure in him.” A little while, a coming one, and the one dividing line of the book drawn inside a prophet's sentence: live by faith, or shrink back. And the preacher closes the movement by refusing to count his people among the shrinkers: “But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.” We are not of those. It is an act of pastoral defiance, the preacher naming his congregation's identity ahead of their performance and calling them to live inside it. The sermon has now issued its warmest invitation and its most terrifying warning within twenty verses of each other, and it regards that not as a contradiction but as the truth about a door that is genuinely open and a cliff that is genuinely there. Next it answers the question the Habakkuk line raises. What does living by faith look like over a lifetime? The answer is a hall of witnesses, forty names deep.

title: By Faith
subtitle: Hebrews 11
description: The roll of the ancients at the writer's own pace: welcomed from afar, the world not worthy of them, and the list left open, together with us.
paragraphs: The sermon now defines its key word and then unleashes a procession. “Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see. This is why the ancients were commended.” Faith is not wishing in this book; it is assurance and certainty aimed at things hoped for and unseen, and it is the quality every honored name in Israel's story turns out to have shared. The roll begins before Israel, with creation itself: “By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible.” Then Abel, whose better sacrifice still speaks though he is dead, faith's first martyr still testifying. Then Enoch, who “was taken up so that he did not see death,” commended as one who pleased God, which prompts the chapter's rule: “And without faith it is impossible to please God. For anyone who approaches Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him.” Then Noah, warned “about things not yet seen,” who in godly fear built an ark on dry land and became an heir of righteousness. The stories have their own books in this series; the sermon races through them in its own compressions, and this telling stays with the sermon's pace, because the accumulation is the argument.

Abraham gets the longest stretch, as he should in a book about promise. “By faith Abraham, when called to go to a place he would later receive as his inheritance, obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going.” Obeyed and went, destination unknown: that is the sermon's portrait of faith in its purest form. He then lived in the promised land itself “as a stranger in a foreign country,” in tents, with Isaac and Jacob, heirs of the same promise living like guests in their own inheritance, “For he was looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God.” Sarah is named in her own right: she “was enabled to conceive a child, because she considered Him faithful who had promised,” and from one man as good as dead came descendants like the stars and the sand. Then the chapter stops the roll and delivers its sober center: “All these people died in faith, without having received the things they were promised. However, they saw them and welcomed them from afar. And they acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth.” Died without receiving. Saw from afar and welcomed. Strangers and exiles by their own confession, “longing for a better country, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them.” Not ashamed to be called their God: the sentence from chapter six about Jesus and his brothers finds its twin here, God's unashamedness toward people whose whole reward was a welcome from a distance.

The roll resumes at the summit of Abraham's testing: he “offered up Isaac on the altar,” reasoning “that God could raise the dead, and in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death,” the promises and the knife held together by a conclusion about God's power. Then the patriarchs pass in single strokes: Isaac blessing, Jacob dying and worshiping over his staff, Joseph on his deathbed giving instructions about his bones, a man in Egypt ordering his burial in a country he had never lived in, because the exodus was as certain to him as his own funeral. Moses dominates the last stretch: hidden by parents unafraid of the king's edict, refusing Pharaoh's household when grown, choosing “to suffer oppression with God’s people rather than to experience the fleeting enjoyment of sin,” valuing “disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt,” leaving Egypt without fearing the king's anger because “he persevered because he saw Him who is invisible,” keeping the Passover, and leading the people through the sea as on dry land. Then Jericho's walls, and Rahab the prostitute of Jericho, welcomed into the roll by the same two words as Abraham: by faith.

And then the preacher runs out of time before he runs out of names. “And what more shall I say? Time will not allow me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets,” who through faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, shut the mouths of lions, quenched fire, escaped the sword, gained strength out of weakness, and saw women receive back their dead. The roll then turns deliberately toward the sufferers: others “were tortured and refused their release, so that they might gain a better resurrection,” endured mocking and flogging, chains and prison, stoning and the sword; one line in the list, being sawn in two, names a death the older books never narrate, carried here on the sermon's own testimony. They wandered “in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, oppressed, and mistreated,” in deserts and caves, and the verdict pronounced over the whole ragged company is the chapter's most startling sentence: “The world was not worthy of them.” The roll ends where it must, unfinished on purpose: “These were all commended for their faith, yet they did not receive what was promised. God had planned something better for us, so that together with us they would be made perfect.” Together with us. The ancients wait for the sermon's own hearers to complete the procession, which means the roll is still open, and the people in the room are its next names.

title: Run with Endurance
subtitle: Hebrews 12:1–17
description: A stadium of witnesses, discipline read as sonship with a harvest later, straight paths for weak knees, and Esau's single meal as the standing warning.
paragraphs: The roll of witnesses does not stay in its chapter. It takes its seats around a stadium. “Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles, and let us run with endurance the race set out for us.” The ancients of chapter eleven become the crowd, and the hearers become the runners, and the sermon's instruction is a runner's: throw off everything that weighs, especially the entangling sin, and run with endurance, because this race is long.
