The eyes have one assigned target: “Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.” Author and perfecter, the faith's pioneer and its finisher, and his method on the worst day of it was joy: he endured the cross for the joy set before him, treating its shame as a small thing. “Consider Him who endured such hostility from sinners, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart.” Weariness and heart-loss are named as the race's real opponents, and considering him is the prescribed defense.

Then the sermon reframes the congregation's pain in a way that could offend if it were not so carefully built. “In your struggle against sin, you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood.” Their struggle is real, and it has not yet cost blood, and the preacher says so to give them scale, not to shame them. What they are enduring has a name they have forgotten, and he quotes it from Proverbs, addressed to them as sons: “My son, do not take lightly the discipline of the Lord, and do not lose heart when He rebukes you. For the Lord disciplines the one He loves, and He chastises every son He receives.” Suffering, in this frame, is not evidence of abandonment but of sonship: “Endure suffering as discipline; God is treating you as sons. For what son is not disciplined by his father?” The alternative is the cold one: no discipline means “you are illegitimate children and not true sons.” Earthly fathers disciplined briefly, as they thought best, and were respected for it; “Should we not much more submit to the Father of our spirits and live?” God's discipline runs “for our good, so that we may share in His holiness,” and its verdict is agricultural and patient: “No discipline seems enjoyable at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it yields a harvest of righteousness and peace to those who have been trained by it.” Painful now, harvest later, and trained is the hinge word: the discipline makes athletes of the people it hurts.

So the pastoral instructions turn physical, the language of a trainer working a tired team. “Therefore strengthen your limp hands and weak knees. Make straight paths for your feet, so that the lame may not be disabled, but rather healed.” Limp hands, weak knees, lame feet: the congregation is pictured as runners in the late miles, and the charge is to straighten up and straighten the path, for their own healing and for the weaker runners behind them. Then the race becomes a road with other travelers on it: “Pursue peace with everyone, as well as holiness, without which no one will see the Lord.” Peace pursued with everyone, holiness pursued without negotiation, and a watch set over the community's roots: “See to it that no one falls short of the grace of God, and that no root of bitterness springs up to cause trouble and defile many.” A root is underground before it is a plant; bitterness in one heart is treated as a congregational contaminant, defiling many, and seeing to it is again the plural work of chapter three's daily exhortation.

The warning of this movement has a face, and it is an old one from Genesis. “See to it that no one is sexually immoral, or is godless like Esau, who for a single meal sold his birthright.” Esau traded the permanent for the immediate, the birthright of the firstborn for one meal eaten once, and the sermon's account of his remorse is the chilling part: “For you know that afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. He could find no ground for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears.” He sought the blessing with tears and could not recover what the meal had cost. The text does not say he sought repentance and was refused it; it says he found no ground to undo the exchange, the blessing gone the way the birthright went, tears notwithstanding. Carried at the sermon's full strength, Esau stands in the book as the warning against one specific transaction: treating the permanent inheritance as small enough to trade for something that can be eaten today. The people being warned had already, in their better days, joyfully accepted the confiscation of their property for the faith's sake. The sermon is asking them to keep valuing the unseen estate above the visible meal, and it has now given them a stadium, a trainer, and a cautionary ancestor to run by.

title: A Kingdom That Cannot Be Shaken
subtitle: Hebrews 12:18–29
description: Not the touchable mountain but Mount Zion already reached, one final shaking of all that can be shaken, and an unshakable kingdom received with awe.
paragraphs: The sermon now sets the two mountains of the two covenants side by side and tells its hearers which one they have come to. The first is Sinai, and it is described the way Exodus describes it, as an assault on every sense. “For you have not come to a mountain that can be touched and that is burning with fire; to darkness, gloom, and storm; to a trumpet blast or to a voice that made its hearers beg that no further word be spoken.” A touchable mountain, tangible, burning, dark, loud, and terrifying past endurance: the command itself was a death sentence on approach, “If even an animal touches the mountain, it must be stoned,” and the sight shook even the mediator: “The sight was so terrifying that even Moses said, ’I am trembling with fear.’” The sermon's hearers know this mountain. It is the mountain of the law they grew up under, the mountain where God was present and the people begged for distance. The preacher's point is not that Sinai was bad. It is that Sinai is not where they now stand.

“Instead, you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.” The sentence then opens like a door into a festival already in progress. “You have come to myriads of angels in joyful assembly, to the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven. You have come to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.” Every item is present tense and already reached: you have come. Angels in festal gathering rather than blasting trumpets. The firstborn enrolled, names on heaven's register, the righteous made perfect, the very company chapter eleven said was waiting to be perfected together with us. God the Judge of all is there, and the sermon does not hide him, but between the hearers and the Judge stands the mediator of the new covenant and his sprinkled blood, and the blood speaks: Abel's blood cried from the ground for vengeance, and this blood speaks a better word. The congregation listening to this sermon, some of them wavering, some of them staying home, are told they have already arrived at this. The drift the book warns against is drift away from a festival, away from a city, away from a better word being spoken over them at this moment.

Precisely because the arrival is real, the old warning returns one last time, and it is the book's final and highest form of it. “See to it that you do not refuse Him who speaks. For if the people did not escape when they refused Him who warned them on earth, how much less will we escape if we reject Him who warns us from heaven?” On earth at Sinai, from heaven now: the speaker is greater in his location and his person, and refusal is correspondingly heavier. His voice once shook the mountain, and the sermon quotes his promise through Haggai: “Once more I will shake not only the earth, but heaven as well.” Once more, one final shaking, and the words signify, the preacher explains, “the removal of what can be shaken,” created things, “so that the unshakable may remain.” Everything made can be shaken, and will be, once. What remains after the shaking is whatever was never made to be shaken, and the hearers' portion is named in the sermon's great summarizing sentence: “Therefore, since we are receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us be filled with gratitude, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe.”

Receiving, present tense, an unshakable kingdom: that is the book's final account of what its hearers hold, and the response it asks for is not relief but reverence. Gratitude, acceptable worship, reverence and awe, because the last line of the movement restores the fire to the festival without apology: “For our God is a consuming fire.” Zion is not Sinai softened. The God of the joyful assembly is the same God who burned on the touchable mountain, and the difference lies not in his temperature but in the mediator and the better-speaking blood standing in the congregation's place. The sermon has reached its summit. What remains is a single chapter of household instruction, love, money, leaders, prayer, and a blessing, spoken to people who now know exactly which mountain they live on and how much of it cannot be shaken.

title: Keep On Loving One Another
subtitle: Hebrews 13
description: Brotherly love continued, angels entertained unawares, outside the camp with him, the God of peace who raised the great Shepherd, and grace as the last word.
paragraphs: The sermon ends the way a letter ends, in a rush of household instruction, and its first line is a command to continue, not to start. “Continue in brotherly love.” The love already exists in this congregation; it is to be kept going. Then hospitality, with its famous reason attached: “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it.” Abraham at his tent door stands behind the sentence unnamed. Then the prisoners: “Remember those in prison as if you were bound with them, and those who are mistreated as if you were suffering with them,” memory done with the body, sympathy as a kind of shared sentence. Marriage is set under the whole community's guard: “Marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.” And money gets the chapter's most-quoted promise as its antidote: “Keep your lives free from the love of money and be content with what you have, for God has said: ’Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.’” Contentment is built on presence, not on supply, and the congregation's answering confession is given for them to say aloud: “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?”

The leaders past and present frame the middle of the chapter. “Remember your leaders who spoke the word of God to you. Consider the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith.” Look at where their lives came out, and copy the faith that got them there. Between that memory and the command to obey the present leaders stands the sermon's one-sentence summary of its entire subject, and it lands almost casually in the middle of the practicalities: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” The unchanging Christ of chapter one, whose years never end, holds steady while teachings blow through: “Do not be carried away by all kinds of strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace and not by foods of no value to those devoted to them.” Grace strengthens hearts; food rules do not, and the altar is redefined in a single stroke: “We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat.”

Then the chapter walks outside the city, following the old rite to its fulfillment. On the Day of Atonement, “the high priest brings the blood of animals into the Holy Place as a sacrifice for sin, the bodies are burned outside the camp.” And so it was with Jesus: “And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood.” Outside the gate, outside the camp, in the place of refuse and disgrace, and the sermon draws the conclusion as an invitation rather than a lament: “Therefore let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore.” Go out to him, and carry the disgrace as he carried it, because the congregation's geography has already been settled in chapter eleven: “For here we do not have a permanent city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.” The sacrifices of the new order are then named, and they are not animals: “Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name. And do not neglect to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased.” Praise from confessing lips, good done, goods shared: these are the offerings of the people whose sin offering is finished forever. Obedience to leaders follows, with its reason, that they “watch over your souls as those who must give an account,” and the leaders' joy is named as the congregation's own advantage.

The letter closes the way its author finally steps out from behind the sermon, in first person and with requests. “Pray for us; we are convinced that we have a clear conscience and desire to live honorably in every way. And I especially urge you to pray that I may be restored to you soon.” Then the blessing rises to the height of the first chapter one more time: “Now may the God of peace, who through the blood of the eternal covenant brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep, equip you with every good thing to do His will.” The God of peace, the blood of the eternal covenant, the great Shepherd brought back from the dead, and equipping as the blessing's content: everything the hearers need to do his will, supplied by the God who asks it. And then the author names his own book with a phrase that tells its readers how the whole thing was meant: “I urge you, brothers, to bear with my word of exhortation, for I have only written to you briefly.” A word of exhortation, briefly: thirteen chapters of the densest argument in the New Testament, called brief by the man who wrote it, because the exhortation was the point all along and the argument was only its engine. News follows in a breath: “Be aware that our brother Timothy has been released. If he arrives soon, I will come with him to see you.” Greetings from the leaders, from all the saints, from those of Italy, and the last word is the one the whole sermon has been about: “Grace be with all of you.” The book that never names its author ends facing its people, and the exhortation is complete.
